newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission warns British firm on nuclear materials.
newsitem.headline: Commission warns British firm on nuclear materials.

text.p: The European Commission has issued a warning to British-based engineering firm Jenson Tungsten Ltd, saying it had failed to respect EU rules on essential safeguard requirements for nuclear materials.
There had been several infringements between 1992 and 1995 of rules laid down in the EU's Euratom treaty, including the lack of a nuclear accounting system "for an unacceptably long time".
It also noted that a discrepancy of 1.466 tonnes of depleted uranium and 7.5 kilograms natural uranium in its stocks had not been satisfactorily explained or justified.
"It is missing or it has been badly booked, that's the two possibilities," an EU official said, adding that the materials concerned could not be used for weapons production.

In its official journal L 313, the Commission ordered the firm to provide it with a report on measures taken to rectify the infringements within three months from November 13, the date of the Commission's decision.
"The warning is imposed with the understanding that the shortcomings with the respect to source documentation, labelling and nuclear materials accounting system be rectified," it said.

Jenson Tungsten operates from premises previously occupied by firms which carried out machining operations on depleted uranium. When it began operating in 1992 it took possession of a residual stock of depleted uranium turnings or 'swarf'.
The firm now works in the field of manufacture and machining of tungsten alloys and there are no longer activities concerning nuclear material on the site, the Commission said.

It said a stock figure of 9.073 tonnes of depleted uranium and 7.5 kilograms of natural uranium had been agreed in 1992 and Jenson Tungsten had confirmed in 1994 that 6.407 tonnes of depleted uranium swarf had been dispatched in October 1993.
However, after a Euratom inspection carried out in April 1995 a discrepeancy became apparent between the stocks established in 1992 and the residual stocks.

"No activities, for example machining of uranium, had taken place," it said. "The best estimate of the residual stock being 1.2 tonnes of depleted uranium, there was a discrepancy of 1.466 tonnes depleted uranium and 7.5 kilograms natural uranium."
In a reply, the company said that the natural uranium had probably been put in with the remainder of the swarf and that the "estimates were necessarily imprecise."
